newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - EMU poses tough jobs questions for Europe.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EMU poses tough jobs questions for Europe.

text.p: Monetary union may make Europe an economic force to be reckoned with, but some analysts say the belt-tightening required may increase unemployment just as traditional safety nets disappear.

Supporters for a single European currency, noting the division of the world into large trading blocs, argue that European firms must be allowed the benefits of trading in their own backyard without the burden of currency exchanges.

Freer market access, lower transaction costs and easier travel between countries are all touted as compelling advantages of European economic and monetary union (EMU) that could actually boost employment across the continent long-term.

Moreover, the reduction in Europe's national debt levels demanded for entry into EMU will free up funds currently absorbed by interest payments. In theory, this could be used to ease Europe's stubbornly high 11 percent unemployment average.

But from the time EMU is launched in 1999, countries which are still able to adjust their national currencies to restore nternational competitiveness will hardly have any say on monetary policy. This could have a drastic effect on employment.

"The main effect of EMU in the short-term is that it takes away a possible safety valve from the labour markets," Steven Englander, international economist at investment bank Smith Barney in Paris said.

Englander said that in the first two years or so after 1999, employment levels could show an initial rise because of the relatively healthy, low-inflation state of the economies of those countries that qualify for EMU.
But after that, the collective wage bargaining systems still employed by a number of countries across Europe could prove too inflexible once the possibility of an exchange rate adjustment is gone.

"What then if a country makes a big mistake in its wage bargaining rounds?" he asked, noting that an excessively high round of wage settlements would lead to that country's products being too expensive.
That in turn could lead to serious job losses unless other compensatory measures were introduced that could be "very slow and very expensive", he said.

All this would be less of a problem if EMU boosted cross-border labour flows which, nearly four years after the creation of the single European market, are still barely noticeable. But there is wide consensus that it will not.

"We do not expect to see vast amounts of cross-border movements just because of EMU," said Norman Bowers, head of employment analysis for the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
"The portability of everything from qualifications to pensions will remain a problem, and then of course language is still an issue," Bowers added.

In a report last July, the OECD said western nations had to face up to the stark choice between persistently high jobless rates or the freeing up of labour markets to create more jobs, while still condeming to poverty some of those in work.

The European labour market, because of the high level of welfare provision and less tangible cultural factors, is widely held by employers to be less flexible than that in, for example, the United States.

That view, hotly disputed by Europe's trade unions and other worker groups, nonetheless appears to have found favour among Europe's governments, a number of which are already putting through measures to free up their labour markets.

Germany, which according to some estimates has labour costs up to double that in comparable U.S. industries, has launched an attack on the generous system of worker benefits once seen as underpinning the country's post-war economic miracle.
France, along with Germany seen as the other vital early entrant to EMU, has sought to cut its overall labour costs with moves to axe thousands of civil service and other public sector jobs.

And Spain, which has the highest jobless rate in Europe, is now moving away from an old labour law under which companies were only justified in making redundancies if their survival was otherwise threatened.
But unions across Europe argue that higher productivity, not flexibility, is the long-term key to jobs creation and that governments should instead invest in measures to enhance Europe's output.

"Over the last decades it has been Germany and Japan that have invested the most in productivity, and that is why their currencies have over the long-term been so strong," Hans-Georg Wehner, management board secretary of Germany's DGB trade union umbrella group.
Wehner said that German labour costs looked high compared to those in the U.S. because of the huge appreciation of the German currency against the dollar since the war.
Declared U.S. figures which currently show unemployment at around 5.5 percent, did not include large numbers of jobless people that were not registered as such, he said.
Wehner said full-employment targets and higher investment in the workforce were more appropriate long-term goals than creating a freer labour market.

But such arguments have fallen on largely deaf ears as far as Europe's decision-makers are concerned, who have so far thwarted efforts by unions and political sympathisers to introduce a specific commitment on employment into the Maastricht Treaty.
If proponents of such policies such as Germany's SPD and Britain's Labour Party come to power in elections due over the next two years that might change.

But whatever the shift in political balance in the run up to EMU, the financial tightness required by the Maastricht criteria limit the scope for manoeuvre. That, some fear, may threaten the jobs of European workforces just as governments start to cut away the safety nets.
